title: Web3 Development with JavaScript & Node.js
tagline: ethers, wallets, signed logins, indexers and tests: the JavaScript half of a Web3 application
summary: Build the JavaScript side of a Web3 application: handle amounts safely with BigInt, read the chain with ethers, send transactions carefully, connect to wallets, build a signed-message login, index events with Node.js and test everything with Hardhat. All Solidity listings were compiled and all JavaScript listings were syntax-checked. You run the code yourself on a local or test network.

modules.title: JavaScript for Web3
modules.summary: The parts of JavaScript Web3 code relies on: BigInt, async functions, hex strings, units and the tooling around them.
modules.outcome: You can handle amounts safely with BigInt and units and write async code that talks to a network.
modules.intro: You do not need to be a JavaScript expert to build Web3 apps, but a few features matter more than usual: numbers that can be bigger than JavaScript's normal limits, code that waits for the network, and strings that are really numbers in hex. This module covers those and sets up the project.

topics.title: Amounts, BigInt and units
topics.html:
JavaScript's normal number type is a floating-point value that is exact only up to about nine quadrillion. One ether is a quintillion wei, far beyond that. Blockchain amounts are therefore handled as BigInt, a built-in type for arbitrarily large whole numbers, written with an n suffix such as 1000000000000000000n. BigInt and normal numbers do not mix in the same calculation, which prevents a silent loss of precision.

Helpers from ethers
FunctionPurpose
parseEther('1.5')Text to wei as BigInt
formatEther(x)BigInt wei to a readable string
parseUnits('12.5', 6)Text to base units for a token with 6 decimals
formatUnits(x, 6)Base units to readable text

Units converter

Change the amount and decimals to see how it is stored. Very large numbers are shown approximately here; real code uses BigInt.

Adjust Human amount, Decimals and see Stored whole number change.

Check what you just learned

1. Why use BigInt for token amounts?
  • It is faster
  • It uses less memory
  • It is required by wallets
  • Normal numbers lose precision beyond about 9 quadrillion (correct)

Precision matters with money.

Check what you just learned

1. BigInt literals end with:
  • n (correct)
  • b
  • i
  • x

For example 10n.
keyPoints: Amounts are BigInt values in the smallest unit.
Convert to text only for display with formatUnits.

topics.title: Async code, hex strings and project set-up
topics.html:
Talking to a blockchain takes time, so almost every call returns a Promise. You write async functions and use await to wait for results. If a call fails, it throws, and you handle that with try and catch. Three habits matter: always await, always catch errors, and never block the page while waiting.

Hex strings
ValueLooks likeMeaning
Address0x5B38Da6a701c568545dCfcB03FcB875f56beddC420 bytes shown as 40 hex digits; checksummed capitals protect against typos
Transaction hash0x followed by 64 hex digitsA fingerprint of a transaction
Function selector0x followed by 8 hex digitsThe first 4 bytes of the hash of the function signature
Quantity in RPC0x1b4A number written in hexadecimal

A sensible starting project

  1. Install Node.js (a current long-term-support version).
  2. Create a folder and run npm init.
  3. Install ethers with npm install ethers.
  4. Keep secrets in a .env file and add it to .gitignore.
  5. Use a free account with a hosted RPC provider or a local test node.
  6. Start on a test network or a local node, never with real funds.

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting await, so you print a Promise instead of the value.
  • Committing a .env file or a private key to a public repository.
  • Doing calculations with Number when values could be large.

Check what you just learned

1. What does forgetting await give you?
  • The value
  • A Promise object that has not finished (correct)
  • An error always
  • A BigInt

You must wait for results.

Check what you just learned

1. A checksummed address helps catch:
  • Reorgs
  • High fees
  • Typing mistakes (correct)
  • Hacks

Capital letters encode a check.
keyPoints: Network calls return Promises: await them and catch errors.
Keep keys in environment variables, never in the repository.

1. Why do view functions cost no gas when called from a script?
  • They are free of code
  • Gas is optional
  • They are cached
  • They are read by a node without a transaction (correct)

Reads need no transaction.

Check what you just learned

1. Events are useful for:
  • Reading history (correct)
  • Paying gas
  • Mining
  • Hiding data

Cheap logs.

Wei

modules.title: Reading the chain with ethers
modules.summary: Providers, contracts, events and the habits of reliable read-only code.
modules.outcome: You can read balances, call view functions, filter events and handle errors in a read-only script.
modules.intro: Reading is the safest thing you can do on a blockchain: no keys, no cost, no risk. It is also where most real applications spend nearly all their time. This module builds a read-only script and explains how to make it reliable.

topics.title: A read-only script
topics.html:
What the script does
StepNotes
JsonRpcProvider(url)Connects to a node or hosted service; the URL often contains an API key, so keep it secret
getNetworkConfirms which chain you are talking to; always check
getBalanceReturns a BigInt in wei
Contract with a human-readable ABILists only the functions and events you need
noteCount and getNoteView calls: free reads
queryFilter with a block rangePast events, in a limited range
main().catch(...)Handles failures and sets an exit code

Check what you just learned

1. Why check getNetwork?
  • It lowers fees
  • To confirm you are on the intended chain (correct)
  • It is required by ethers
  • It signs messages

Wrong-chain bugs are common.

Watch out

An RPC URL with an API key is a secret. If it leaks, others can use your quota.

Check what you just learned

1. A human-readable ABI lists:
  • Keys
  • Everything ever
  • Only what you need (correct)
  • Fees

Short and clear.
keyPoints: A provider is a read connection; a contract wraps the ABI.
Always confirm the network and handle errors.

topics.title: Events and block ranges
topics.html:
Events are how contracts publish history. Each log has the contract address, indexed topics for fast filtering and non-indexed data. You can ask for all logs of a given event in a range of blocks, filtered by indexed arguments such as the author. Most RPC providers limit the size of a range or the number of results, so serious code reads in batches.

Event reading pitfalls
ProblemRemedy
Querying from block 0 to the latest in one callRead in batches of a few hundred or thousand blocks
Provider returns an error for too many resultsNarrow the range or the filter
Missing events during a gapSave the last block you have processed and continue from the next
Duplicates after a restartUse a unique key of transaction hash and log index
Events from the latest blocks vanish after a reorganisationWait for confirmations before treating events as final

Check what you just learned

1. Why wait for confirmations before trusting recent events?
  • To save bandwidth
  • Providers require it
  • Events are encrypted
  • Recent blocks can be replaced in a reorganisation (correct)

Finality takes time.

Check what you just learned

1. A reorganisation is when:
  • Recent blocks are replaced by a different chain tip (correct)
  • Fees rise
  • A contract is deleted
  • A wallet locks

The latest blocks can change.
keyPoints: Read events in batches and remember where you stopped.
Use unique keys and wait for confirmations.

topics.title: Reliability: limits, retries and caching
topics.html:
Why shared reading wins

Change the users and polling rate to see daily requests if every browser polls, compared with one backend reading each block. A teaching model.

Adjust Users, Polls per minute per user and see Browser polling (requests per day), One backend (requests per day) change.

Habits of reliable read code
HabitWhy
Cache values that do not change quicklyFewer requests, faster pages
Use a backend to share reads between many usersStays inside provider limits
Retry with increasing delays (backoff)Networks are flaky
Set timeoutsA hung request should not freeze the page
Use more than one provider for important dataProviders have outages
Show stale data with a notice rather than nothingBetter user experience

Common mistakes

  • Polling from every browser every second.
  • Treating a failed read as 'no data' instead of an error.
  • Ignoring rate-limit responses.

Check what you just learned

1. What is backoff?
  • Cancelling a request
  • Waiting longer after each failed attempt (correct)
  • Changing the chain
  • Hiding errors

A polite retry.

Check what you just learned

1. Timeouts prevent:
  • Reorgs
  • Gas fees
  • A hung request freezing the app (correct)
  • Hacks

A hung request should fail quickly.

Key terms: flip and sort

Provider
A read connection to a chain
ABI
The description of a contract's interface
Event log
A record emitted by a contract
Confirmation
A block built on top of yours
Reorganisation
Replacement of recent blocks
Backoff
Increasing waits between retries
keyPoints: Cache, share reads through a backend and retry with backoff.
Show stale data honestly rather than an empty page.

modules.title: Sending transactions
modules.summary: Signers, simulation, gas estimation, nonces, receipts and a complete error-handling pattern.
modules.outcome: You can send a transaction from a script, simulate it first, wait for confirmations and handle failures.
modules.intro: Reading is safe; writing costs money and cannot be undone. This module teaches the careful sequence professionals follow: simulate, estimate, send, wait and handle every way it can fail.

topics.title: A careful send script
topics.html:
Watch out

Use a throw-away test account on a test network. Never put a key that controls real funds in a script, a shared machine or a repository.

Check what you just learned

1. Why simulate with staticCall before sending?
  • It is cheaper than reading
  • It skips the wallet
  • It signs the call
  • It finds out whether the call would revert before you pay for it (correct)

Avoid paying for a failure.

Check what you just learned

1. A receipt with status 0 means the transaction:
  • Reverted (correct)
  • Succeeded
  • Is pending
  • Is cancelled

It failed on-chain.
keyPoints: Simulate, estimate, send, wait, then check the receipt.
Keys come from the environment and belong to test accounts only.

topics.title: Nonces, gas and stuck transactions
topics.html:
Key ideas
IdeaMeaning
NonceThe count of transactions an account has sent; each must use the next number in order
Gas limitThe most gas a transaction may use; unused gas is returned
Max fee and priority feeWhat you are willing to pay per unit of gas in total and as a tip for the block producer
PendingWaiting to be included
ReplacementA new transaction with the same nonce and a higher fee replaces a stuck one
CancelReplace a stuck transaction with a zero-value transfer to yourself using the same nonce

If a transaction is stuck

  1. Do not send many new ones; they queue behind the stuck nonce.
  2. Check the fee against current network conditions.
  3. Resubmit the same nonce with a higher fee.
  4. Or replace it with a harmless transaction to yourself.
  5. Tell the user clearly what is happening and show the transaction link.

Fee calculator

Change gas used, price and ETH price to see the cost of one transaction. Teaching figures.

Adjust Gas used, Gas price (gwei), ETH price (rupees) and see Fee (ETH), Fee (rupees) change.

Check what you just learned

1. Why do later transactions wait behind a stuck one?
  • Fees are high
  • Nonces must be used in order (correct)
  • Wallets refuse
  • Blocks are full

Order is enforced.

Check what you just learned

1. A gas limit protects you by:
  • Cancelling retries
  • Raising the price
  • Capping the maximum gas used (correct)
  • Hiding errors

It sets a ceiling on gas used.
keyPoints: Nonces enforce order; stuck transactions are replaced by raising the fee on the same nonce.
Estimate gas and add a margin.

topics.title: Receipts, errors and user messages
topics.html:
Common error codes in ethers v6
CodeMeaningWhat to tell the user
INSUFFICIENT_FUNDSNot enough currency for value plus gasAdd more currency and try again
CALL_EXCEPTIONThe contract revertedShow the contract's reason in plain words
ACTION_REJECTEDThe user declined in the walletNo problem; try again when ready
NONCE_EXPIREDThat nonce was already usedRefresh and try again
REPLACEMENT_UNDERPRICEDA replacement needs a higher feeIncrease the fee or wait
NETWORK_ERROR / TIMEOUTThe node did not answerRetry shortly

A receipt tells you what happened on the chain: the block, the gas used, the status and the logs. Always check the status, because a transaction that was mined but reverted still costs gas. Decode logs to show results such as the id of a new item.

Common mistakes

  • Assuming the transaction succeeded because the hash was returned.
  • Showing raw error objects to users.
  • Not telling the user what to do next.

Check what you just learned

1. If the user presses Reject in the wallet, you should:
  • Show a scary error
  • Log them out
  • Resend automatically
  • Treat it as a normal choice and let them retry (correct)

A rejection is not a failure.

Check what you just learned

1. A mined but reverted transaction:
  • Still costs gas (correct)
  • Costs nothing
  • Is cancelled
  • Is a success

Gas is spent.

Key terms: flip and sort

Signer
An object that can sign and send
Nonce
A per-account transaction counter
Gas limit
The maximum gas a transaction may use
Receipt
The record of a mined transaction
staticCall
A simulation that sends nothing
Replacement
Overwriting a stuck transaction
keyPoints: Check the receipt status and decode logs.
Translate error codes into friendly next steps.

modules.title: Wallets and signing
modules.summary: Connecting to browser wallets, chain switching, signed messages and passwordless login.
modules.outcome: You can connect to a wallet, handle account and chain changes and build a safe signed-message login.
modules.intro: A wallet is the user's identity and key chain. Your app never sees their private key; it asks the wallet to sign. This module covers connecting, reacting to changes and using signatures to log users in without passwords.

topics.title: Connecting to a wallet
topics.html:
Pieces of the connection
PieceRole
window.ethereumThe provider injected by the wallet (EIP-1193)
eth_requestAccountsAsks the user to share an account; they may refuse
BrowserProvider and getSignerethers objects that route requests through the wallet
wallet_switchEthereumChainAsks the wallet to change networks
accountsChanged and chainChangedEvents your app must handle

Common mistakes

  • Assuming the user is on the right network.
  • Ignoring the accountsChanged event and showing the wrong account.
  • Requesting a connection on page load instead of after a user click.

Check what you just learned

1. Why should the app listen to accountsChanged?
  • To save gas
  • The user can switch accounts at any time (correct)
  • It is required by law
  • It signs messages

Keep the page in step with the wallet.

Check what you just learned

1. The app should request accounts:
  • Never
  • On every page load silently
  • After a user action (correct)
  • Using the private key

Ask politely.
keyPoints: Connect through the wallet's injected provider and ask for permission.
React to account and chain changes.

topics.title: Signing messages safely
topics.html:
Kinds of signature
KindUsed forRisk
Message signature (personal_sign)Login, proving control of an addressA signed message must not be reusable elsewhere
Typed data (EIP-712)Orders, permits, votes with readable fieldsUsers must read the fields
Transaction signatureActually changing the chainCosts gas and moves value

Signing a message costs nothing and moves no funds, but it can still be dangerous if the message authorises something elsewhere. A signature on an opaque hash can be an approval hidden in plain sight. Good apps show human-readable text, bind it to a domain and a time and add a single-use nonce.

Rules for signing prompts

  1. Show text a person can read.
  2. Say what the signature is for.
  3. Include the domain.
  4. Include a nonce and a time.
  5. Never request signatures on arbitrary data from untrusted sources.
  6. Never ask users for their recovery phrase.

Check what you just learned

1. What risk does an opaque hash signature carry?
  • It costs gas
  • It is encrypted
  • It is slow
  • It might authorise something the user did not understand (correct)

Readable messages protect users.

Check what you just learned

1. A signature that includes the domain helps stop:
  • Another site reusing it (correct)
  • High fees
  • Reorgs
  • Typos

Domain binding.
keyPoints: Message signatures cost nothing but must be readable and bound to context.
Typed data (EIP-712) makes fields visible in the wallet.

topics.title: Passwordless login
topics.html:
What each check prevents
CheckPrevents
Nonce exists and is deleted after useReplay of an old signature
Nonce expiryUsing a stale signature later
Domain in the messageA phishing site collecting signatures for yours
Recovered address, not a claimed addressSomeone pretending to be another address
Session expiryEndless access from one signature

Check what you just learned

1. Why recover the address from the signature rather than trust the one the browser sends?
  • It is faster
  • Anyone can claim any address; only the signature proves control (correct)
  • It saves bandwidth
  • It is required by Express

Proof, not claims.

Tip

For production use, follow the Sign-In with Ethereum standard (EIP-4361) and a maintained library instead of writing the message format yourself.

Check what you just learned

1. After use, the nonce should be:
  • Published
  • Reused
  • Deleted (correct)
  • Extended

Single use.

Key terms: flip and sort

EIP-1193
The standard wallet provider interface
Signer
An object that signs for an account
personal_sign
Signing a text message
EIP-712
Signing structured data
Nonce
A single-use number
SIWE
Sign-In with Ethereum
keyPoints: Issue a nonce, sign a readable message, verify and delete the nonce.
Recover the signer from the signature; never trust a claimed address.

modules.title: Node.js backends for Web3
modules.summary: What belongs on a server, a safe event indexer, APIs and keeping everything repeatable.
modules.outcome: You can decide where each responsibility belongs, write a repeat-safe indexer and design a small API over indexed data.
modules.intro: Chains are slow to search and strict about cost. Most real applications add a backend to index events, send e-mails, rate-limit abuse and keep secrets. This module shows what belongs there and how to build it safely.

topics.title: What belongs where
topics.html:
Where each responsibility goes
ResponsibilityBrowserBackendContract
Hold the user's keysWallet onlyNeverNever
Enforce rules that move moneyNoNoYes
Search and filter historyNo (too slow)Yes, via an indexNo
Hold API keys and secretsNeverYesNever
Send e-mail or notificationsNoYesNo
Show progress to the userYesHelpsNo
Rate-limit abuseNoYesNo

A common mistake is to put a rule in the page that should be in the contract (anyone can bypass the page) or to put a secret in the page that should be on the server (anyone can read the page). Treat the browser as untrusted, the backend as your trusted helper and the contract as the final judge.

Check what you just learned

1. Why must money rules live in the contract?
  • It is cheaper
  • Contracts are faster
  • Wallets demand it
  • A page or server can be bypassed; the contract is the final judge (correct)

Do not rely on the front end to enforce rules.

Check what you just learned

1. API keys for an RPC provider belong:
  • On the backend (correct)
  • In the page
  • In the contract
  • In a comment

Keep them private.
keyPoints: Contracts enforce rules; backends index and protect secrets; browsers show and sign.
Treat the browser as untrusted.

topics.title: A repeat-safe indexer
topics.html:
Why it is written this way
FeatureReason
CONFIRMATIONSDo not store events from blocks that could still be replaced
Batches of BATCH blocksStay inside provider limits
indexer_state with last_blockResume exactly where it stopped
A database transaction around events and the new last_blockEither both are saved or neither
INSERT IGNORE with a unique keyRunning the same range twice causes no duplicates
Sleeping about one blockAvoids hammering the provider

The core idea is idempotence: you can run the same step again and get the same result. Crashes, restarts and retries are normal, so any step that cannot be safely repeated is a bug waiting for a bad day.

Check what you just learned

1. Why wrap the inserts and the last_block update in one database transaction?
  • To make it slower
  • So a crash cannot leave events saved but the position unsaved, or the reverse (correct)
  • Databases require it
  • To hide errors

All or nothing.

Check what you just learned

1. Idempotent means:
  • Encrypted
  • Very fast
  • Repeating gives the same result (correct)
  • One time only

Safe to retry.
keyPoints: Index with confirmations, batches and unique keys.
Make every step safe to repeat.

topics.title: APIs, security and operations
topics.html:
Designing the API over your index

  • Expose read endpoints such as notes by author, with pagination.
  • Validate every input and limit page sizes.
  • Require login for anything personal.
  • Apply rate limits per address and per network address.
  • Return clear errors, not stack traces.
  • Never expose database errors or secrets.
Operations checklist
AreaPractice
SecretsEnvironment variables or a secret manager; rotate on suspicion
MonitoringAlert when the indexer falls behind or the provider fails
LoggingLog transaction hashes and error codes, never private keys
BackupsBack up the database; the chain is the source of truth for events
ProvidersHave a second provider for failover
DependenciesUpdate and audit packages regularly

Common mistakes

  • Trusting the browser to tell the server who the user is.
  • Running the indexer once manually and forgetting it.
  • Letting the API return unlimited rows.

Check what you just learned

1. What should alert you in an indexer?
  • Nothing
  • A busy day
  • A new block
  • It falls far behind the latest block or errors repeatedly (correct)

You need to know when it stops.

Check what you just learned

1. The chain remains the source of truth for:
  • Events and balances (correct)
  • Your passwords
  • E-mails
  • CSS

The database is a copy.

Key terms: flip and sort

Indexer
A service that copies events into a database
Idempotent
Safe to repeat
Pagination
Returning results in pages
Rate limit
A cap on requests
Failover
Switching to a backup
Source of truth
The authoritative record
keyPoints: Validate, paginate, rate-limit and log carefully.
Monitor lag and keep secrets out of logs.

modules.title: Testing and tooling
modules.summary: Hardhat tests with ethers, JavaScript unit tests, fork tests, configuration and a security checklist.
modules.outcome: You can write contract tests in JavaScript, configure Hardhat safely and choose the right kind of test.
modules.intro: Code that touches money is tested more thoroughly than most. In the JavaScript world that means Hardhat for contracts, ordinary test frameworks for your helpers and a few end-to-end checks for the whole path.

topics.title: Testing contracts with Hardhat
topics.html:
What the tests check
TestWhy
Stores a note and emits an eventCore behaviour and the event the indexer depends on
Rejects empty and over-long textBoundaries are where bugs live
Records different authorsmsg.sender is used correctly

Habits for good contract tests

  1. Test failures as carefully as successes.
  2. Test boundaries: zero, one, maximum and one over.
  3. Test every event your off-chain code relies on.
  4. Use fresh state for each test with beforeEach.
  5. Name tests after the behaviour they protect.

Check what you just learned

1. Why test the event as well as the stored value?
  • Events are free
  • Your indexer relies on the event (correct)
  • Wallets demand it
  • It is shorter

Off-chain code trusts events.

Check what you just learned

1. beforeEach gives each test:
  • A bank
  • Real funds
  • Fresh state (correct)
  • A key

Independent tests.
keyPoints: Hardhat runs contracts on a local chain for fast tests.
Test boundaries, failures and events.

topics.title: Configuration, forks and other tests
topics.html:
Kinds of test for a Web3 app
KindFindsTool
Contract testsLogic errors in contractsHardhat or Foundry
JavaScript unit testsBugs in helpers: formatting, retries, parsingA test framework such as Jest, Vitest or Mocha
Fork testsProblems with real deployed contractsA local fork of a real network
End-to-end testsBroken user flowsA browser test tool with a test wallet
Manual reviewConfusing wording and risky flowsPeople

A fork runs a local copy of a real network at a chosen block. You can interact with real deployed contracts and see how your code behaves without spending anything. Forks are excellent for testing integrations, but remember that they are a snapshot, not a guarantee about the live network later.

Check what you just learned

1. What is a fork test?
  • A test of cutlery
  • A deployment
  • A hard fork of a chain
  • A local copy of a real network used for testing (correct)

Real contracts, no cost.

Watch out

Keep keys in environment variables. Add .env to .gitignore before the first commit, and check that a private key was never pushed.

Check what you just learned

1. A fork lets you test against:
  • Real deployed contracts at no cost (correct)
  • Real funds
  • Nothing
  • A different language

Great for integrations.
keyPoints: Configure networks with environment variables.
Combine contract, unit, fork and end-to-end tests.

topics.title: Release discipline
topics.html:
Before you release
AreaCheck
ContractsTests pass, coverage reviewed, independent review for anything holding value
FrontendNetwork and address are right; errors are friendly; no secrets in the bundle
BackendRate limits, input validation, monitoring and backups in place
KeysDeployment keys on hardware wallets; test keys separate
DocsA README with set-up, environment variables and a security contact
UsersClear risk disclosure; no promises of profit
Tip

Write the README as if you will hand the project to a stranger tomorrow. Often, that stranger is you in six months.

Check what you just learned

1. Why launch small first?
  • It looks modest
  • It limits harm from anything the tests missed (correct)
  • It lowers gas
  • It avoids reviews

Reduce the blast radius.

Check what you just learned

1. A README should include:
  • Passwords
  • Private keys
  • Set-up and environment variables (correct)
  • Nothing

Help the next person.

Key terms: flip and sort

Hardhat
A development environment for contracts
